label: Projective d-space
notes: This chapter generalises the projective plane to arbitrary dimension d and uses real projective three-space as its working laboratory. Tell students the recurring questions: what survives the jump from plane to space, why lines now need six coordinates, and how a single labelled exterior calculus handles join and meet uniformly across all ranks.

label: Homogeneous coordinates in R^{d+1}
notes: Anchor the construction: a point of d-dimensional projective space is a one-dimensional subspace of the (d plus one)-dimensional vector space, equivalently a nonzero vector up to nonzero scale. Stress that scale freedom is the whole point, and that the finite affine chart is just the slice where the last coordinate equals one.

label: Subspaces and hyperplanes
notes: Walk through the rank dictionary in three-space: rank one points, rank two lines, rank three planes, rank four numbers. Emphasise that a k-dimensional projective subspace comes from a (k plus one)-dimensional linear subspace, and that hyperplanes are the codimension-one dual objects represented by covectors.

label: Join and meet
notes: Introduce join as the smallest subspace containing both operands and meet as their intersection. Connect each to the exterior calculus: join combines disjoint label sets and raises rank, meet is the dual operation that lowers rank once the ambient dimension is subtracted. Promise the dimension formula on the next slide ties them together.

label: The dimension formula
notes: This is the central theorem. Walk students through the two regimes in three-space: two skew lines span everything and meet emptily, while two coplanar lines drop their span to a plane and gain a common point. The formula is the projective analogue of inclusion-exclusion for vector subspace dimensions.

label: Incidence and duality
notes: Duality exchanges points and hyperplanes while reversing join and meet. Show that point lies on hyperplane exactly when the bracket pairing vanishes, and that this incidence is preserved by the inverse-transpose action on covectors. In three-space the self-dual middle object is the line.

label: RP^3: points, lines, planes
notes: Make three-space concrete. Points are rank one, planes are the dual rank three objects, and lines sit in the self-dual middle. Highlight that a plane through the affine equation a x plus b y plus c z plus d uses the four triple labels, and that joining a point with it returns the equation value as a single scalar.

label: Plucker coordinates of a line
notes: Define the six Plucker coordinates as the two-by-two minors of the four-by-two matrix of two point representatives. Stress homogeneity: resampling the same line by a different spanning pair only rescales the six-vector. The labels involving index four record how the line sits relative to the plane at infinity.

label: Grassmann-Plucker and the Klein quadric
notes: Not every six-vector is a line. Decomposability is detected by the single quadratic Grassmann-Plucker relation, an identity for genuine joins and a working test otherwise. Geometrically the relation cuts out the Klein quadric in five-dimensional projective space, so lines of three-space are exactly its points.

label: The bracket in 3-space
notes: The bracket of four points is the four-by-four determinant of their representatives. It vanishes precisely when the four points are coplanar, and its sign and magnitude encode oriented volume. Frame the bracket as the universal incidence and dependence detector that powers every join and meet computation in the chapter.

label: Parallel planes meet at infinity
notes: Projective space removes the parallel exception. Two parallel planes differ only in their constant label, and their meet is a genuine line whose coordinates with index four vanish, identical up to scale to the join of two direction points. This is the payoff of treating points at infinity as ordinary elements.

label: Recap and projection lab
notes: Recap the through-line: one homogeneous principle, the dimension formula governing join and meet, duality pairing points with hyperplanes, and six-coordinate lines living on the Klein quadric. Close with the camera lab, where a three-by-four matrix projects space lines to image lines and direction points to vanishing points.
